title: Ahaz Buys Assyria's Help and Remodels the Temple
summary: Ahaz of Judah abandons the ways of David, sacrifices his son in the fire, and worships at the high places. Threatened by Aram and Israel together, he declares himself Tiglath-pileser's servant and pays him with the temple's silver and gold, and Assyria crushes Damascus. On a visit to Damascus Ahaz sees an altar he admires, has a copy built in Jerusalem, pushes the LORD's bronze altar aside, and strips and rearranges the temple's furnishings on account of the king of Assyria.
story: Chapter 15 closed with a warning: the LORD had begun to send Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel against Judah. Here the pressure arrives, and Judah's king responds by trusting Assyria instead of the LORD. The chapter is a hinge in the book. Until now Judah's kings have been graded as mostly good with the high places remaining; Ahaz is the first king of Judah in about a century, since Ahaziah (8:27), to be judged without any qualification, and his sins match the worst of the north. He also brings the temple itself under the influence of a foreign power. The chapter prepares for the fall of Samaria in chapter 17 and for the great contrast of chapters 18 to 20, where Ahaz's son Hezekiah faces the same empire and trusts the LORD instead.
historical:
Ahaz reigned in the 730s and 720s BC; common reckonings place his reign from about 735 to 715 BC, though the synchronisms with Hezekiah make exact dates contested. The attack in verse 5 is often called the Syro-Ephraimite war (Ephraim being another name for the northern kingdom), dated around 734 to 732 BC. Rezin and Pekah seem to have wanted Judah in a coalition against Assyria, and when Ahaz refused they tried to replace him with a king of their own choosing (Isaiah 7:6). Isaiah 7 records the prophet's meeting with Ahaz during this crisis, urging him to stand firm in faith and not fear the two kings.

Ahaz chose Assyria instead, and it came at once. Tiglath-pileser took Damascus in 732 BC, executed Rezin, and deported the Arameans, ending the kingdom that had troubled Israel since the days of Ahab. An Assyrian inscription lists Jehoahaz of Judah, the fuller form of Ahaz's name, among the kings who paid tribute. Kir, where the Arameans were deported, was their ancestral homeland according to Amos 9:7, and Amos 1:5 had predicted this very exile. The priest Uriah of verses 10-16 is probably the same Uriah whom Isaiah called as a reliable witness (Isaiah 8:2), though that identification can't be proved.
cultural:
Ahaz's message in verse 7, “I am your servant and your son”, is the language of vassal treaties. A weaker king pledged loyalty and service to a great king, who in return offered protection. In Judah's own covenant tradition, the king of the line of David was called God's son (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7). By offering himself as Tiglath-pileser's son, Ahaz transfers that loyalty. The gift of verse 8 is called by a word that normally means a bribe.

The new altar belongs to the same world of power and prestige. Whether the Damascus altar was Assyrian or Aramean in style is debated, and so is whether Assyria required vassals to adopt its worship; many scholars now think it generally did not, which would make Ahaz's changes his own choice to impress his overlord. The large altar became the center of the regular morning and evening offerings, while the LORD's bronze altar, made in Solomon's time, was set to the side for the king's private inquiries. The bronze stands, the basins, and the great bronze Sea resting on twelve oxen (1 Kings 7:23-39) were stripped, probably for their metal to pay tribute. Sacrificing a son in the fire, described in verse 3, was a practice the law explicitly forbade (Deuteronomy 18:10) and linked with the peoples the LORD had driven out.
literary: The chapter is framed by the usual regnal formulas (verses 1-4 and 19-20), but the verdict in verse 2 is unusually blunt: unlike David his father, he did not do what was right. The body has two panels. The first (verses 5-9) is political: threat, appeal, payment, rescue. The second (verses 10-18) is religious and is told in close, almost inventory-like detail: the altar's model, its construction, the king's offerings, the relocation of the old altar, the orders to the priest, the dismantling of the furnishings. The detail itself is the point. The narrator lingers over each change to the house of the LORD so that the reader sees the temple being redesigned around a foreign king. The phrase "on account of the king of Assyria" in verse 18 ties the two panels together.

outline.t: Aram and Israel attack; Ahaz appeals to Assyria

doctrines.note: Ahaz's idolatry is not only bowing to other gods but reshaping the worship of the LORD to suit a human power. The temple still stands and sacrifices still go on, yet the center of gravity has moved to Damascus and Nineveh.

Read alongside Isaiah 7, the chapter is a study in misplaced trust. Ahaz was offered the LORD's promise and chose a treaty instead. What he feared was real, but what he trusted cost him the temple's treasures and his people's independence.
The LORD's altar and furnishings were made according to his instructions. Replacing them with a design copied from another nation's worship treats holy things as matters of royal taste.

words.note: Tavnit, pattern or plan. It is the word used when God showed Moses the pattern of the tabernacle (Exodus 25:9, 40) and when David gave Solomon the plan for the temple (1 Chronicles 28:11). Here the pattern comes from Damascus, and the priest builds according to the king's instructions rather than God's. The choice of word sharpens the irony.
Demut, likeness or model. The same word appears in Genesis 1:26 for humanity made in God's likeness. Here it is only a scale drawing of an altar, but it marks what Ahaz wants his worship to resemble.

Shochad, a gift given to buy favor, usually translated bribe. The law forbids judges to take it (Exodus 23:8). The narrator's choice of this word for Ahaz's payment to Tiglath-pileser tells us how to see it: not diplomacy but purchase, paid with treasures that belonged to the LORD's house.

christ: The most important link to Christ stands just outside this chapter. During the very crisis described in verse 5, Isaiah met Ahaz and offered him a sign from the LORD. When Ahaz refused, Isaiah announced that a young woman (or virgin; the Hebrew word is debated) would conceive and bear a son and call him Immanuel, God with us (Isaiah 7:14). The sign had meaning in Ahaz's own day, since Isaiah said the threat from Aram and Israel would pass before the child grew up, and Matthew 1:23 sees its fullest meaning in the birth of Jesus. The contrast is sharp: Ahaz called himself the son of the Assyrian king to be saved, and God answered with the promise of a son who would be God with his people. Ahaz's remodeled altar also makes the reader long for true worship, which the New Testament finds in Christ, the one sacrifice that needs no human redesign.

hard.q: Did Ahaz really sacrifice his son, and if so how could a king of David's line do such a thing?
hard.a:
The Hebrew says literally that Ahaz made his son pass through the fire. Some interpreters have argued that this describes a dedication ritual in which a child passed near or through flames without being killed. Most scholars read it as actual child sacrifice, because the parallel in 2 Chronicles 28:3 speaks of him burning his sons, because Deuteronomy 12:31 describes the nations burning their children in the fire to their gods, and because the prophets treat the practice as the shedding of innocent blood (Jeremiah 7:31; Ezekiel 16:20-21). The BSB translation reflects that majority reading.

How a Davidic king could do it is the chapter's point. In moments of desperate threat, ancient kings sometimes offered their children to secure divine help (compare the king of Moab in 3:27). Ahaz, facing two armies, turned to the gods of the nations and the power of Assyria instead of the LORD. The narrator does not soften it. The line of David, through which God had promised his kingdom, was capable of the worst sins of the peoples around it, and the book makes clear that the promise survived because of God's faithfulness, not the kings'.

questions: Ahaz faced a real threat and chose a solution he could see over a promise he could not. Where are you tempted to buy security in ways that cost you your faithfulness?
The temple kept its sacrifices even as its center moved toward Assyria. How can worship continue outwardly while its real loyalty shifts elsewhere?
Ahaz called himself the servant and son of a foreign king. Whose approval shapes your decisions most, and how would you know?
